subject: Archaeology
title: The Bust of Nefertiti
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Bust of Nefertiti.

hook.text: In 1912, a German team in Egypt uncovered a painted limestone bust so beautiful it stunned the world.

buildup.text: The bust depicted Queen Nefertiti with perfect symmetry and one mysteriously missing eye.

discovery.text: The 3,300-year-old sculpture was found in a sculptor's workshop — likely a model, not a finished piece.

twist.text: Germany took it to Berlin. Egypt has demanded its return for over a century and been refused every time.

climax.text: The bust is now the most visited artifact in Berlin. Egypt calls it a stolen cultural treasure.

punchline.text: A sculptor's rough draft became one of the most fought-over artworks on earth.

quiz.question: What was the Nefertiti bust likely used for originally?
options: It was placed in Nefertiti's tomb as a burial object
It was a sculptor's workshop model, not a finished piece
It was a religious idol worshipped in temples

details.summary: The painted limestone bust of Queen Nefertiti, created around 1345 BCE and discovered at Amarna in 1912, is one of the most recognized artworks from antiquity. Now displayed in Berlin's Neues Museum, it has been the subject of a century-long repatriation dispute between Germany and Egypt.
details.whyItMatters: The Nefertiti bust is both an artistic masterpiece and a symbol of cultural property disputes. Its location in Berlin rather than Egypt exemplifies the unresolved legacy of colonial-era artifact acquisition.
takeaways: A 3,350-year-old painted bust discovered at Amarna in 1912
It is one of the most iconic works of ancient art worldwide
Egypt has sought its return from Berlin for over a century

faq.question: How did the Nefertiti bust end up in Berlin?
faq.answer: German archaeologist Ludwig Borchardt excavated it in 1912 under a finds-sharing agreement with Egypt. Egypt claims the bust's significance was deliberately downplayed to secure it in the German share. Germany maintains the export was legal under the rules then in force.

faq.question: Why is the bust so well preserved after 3,350 years?
faq.answer: The bust was found face-down in the ruins of the sculptor Thutmose's workshop at Amarna. It was carved from limestone and covered with painted plaster. Dry Egyptian conditions preserved the pigments remarkably well, though the left eye inlay was never installed.
